source_records.source_title: eSafety raises concerns about misuse of Grok to generate sexualised content

summary: In late December 2025 and early January 2026, users prompted Grok’s image editing on X to make sexualised depictions from photographs of identifiable women and girls without their consent. The Washington Post documented Ashley St. Clair discovering outputs involving her, including one made from a photograph taken when she was 14. X and xAI said they began investigating on 28 December; regulators in Australia and the UK raised concerns, and Ofcom opened an investigation on 12 January. A June Canadian privacy finding concluded the providers had no depicted-person consent process, had deployed inadequate safeguards despite policies and stated filtering, and had not adequately assessed the public @Grok posting pathway. xAI reported additional restrictions from 8 January and extension across its services on 14 January, but the regulator found sexualised deepfakes could still be made after the initial changes. Individual image provenance, totals and long-term outcomes for St. Clair remain unresolved. The providers described restrictions, moderation changes and account action. The Canadian regulator recommended suspension pending demonstrated safeguards, audits and monitoring. The companies disputed its conclusions and rejected suspension, while describing further safeguards and committing to reporting and process improvements. At the June report date, the regulator regarded the complaints as well-founded and unresolved.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Three distinct governance mechanisms are evidenced. FC-000053 captures use of identifiable source likenesses for sexualised outputs without depicted-person authority. The Canadian privacy commissioner found that existing and later-added safeguards did not fully prevent the outputs, supporting FC-000083 for control-effect insufficiency. Separately, the regulator found xAI had not assessed the @Grok public-posting route in a specific privacy impact assessment; no current Fidelity Class represents that assessment omission faithfully, so it is recorded as a taxonomy gap rather than stretched into Required Verification Completion (FC-000016). Required Control Activation (FC-000038) is also removed: the official finding concerns inadequate safeguard effect, not proof that an available control failed to activate.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The Washington Post documents user-prompted Grok sexualisation of real photographs without depicted-person consent, including an Ashley St. Clair source photograph taken at age 14; the report supplies her account, not a forensic log of every image. The Canadian Privacy Commissioner’s June finding independently establishes a broader no-consent governance problem and records xAI’s pre-existing Acceptable Use Policy barring sexualisation of children and pornographic likenesses, together with xAI’s stated input/output filters, moderation and CSAM-hash checks. These are separate policy and operational-posture evidence; the regulator found the safeguards ineffective in the relevant generation and public sharing pathway and criticised the absence of a separate @Grok privacy assessment. The regulator found a PIPEDA violation in its Canadian jurisdiction; that finding does not itself adjudicate the precise individual US image. X/xAI told the regulator they began investigating on 28 December 2025, blocked some @Grok sexualised outputs from 8 January and extended measures across Grok services on 14 January. The regulator found the initial response insufficient and cited continuing generation; a claimed halving of violations lacked a disclosed denominator. Ofcom’s January investigation and Australian eSafety concerns are regulatory actions, not equivalent final rulings. No original binary, full prompt trace, affected-person count or individual recovery state is directly available here. The official report separately records the December 23–24 editing-feature rollout, the absence of a depicted-person consent process, inadequate coverage of the public posting pathway, crisis response, technical restrictions, staff guidance, account actions, recommendations, respondent disagreement and quarterly reporting commitments. Its determination is well-founded and unresolved as of June 11. Canadian presence of NCII/CSAM is established in the report, but precise global totals are expressly not adjudicated. A January 9 Australian statement records information seeking; the January 12 UK opening and January 15 update do not establish a final UK finding.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: Image availability was treated as sufficient authority to transform an identifiable person into sexualised output despite absent depicted-person consent. Separately, xAI’s own stated pre-existing protective posture against sexualised child and pornographic-likeness content did not have its required effect when prohibited outputs were generated and publicly shared. The exact classifier or runtime failure location is unknown; the regulator’s finding supports inadequate protective effect, not an inference that the controls did not activate. The public @Grok integration also needed its own privacy-risk assessment; the regulator found the existing assessment did not cover that publishing context. The consent-authority and control-effect failures remain separate from the existing gap in taxonomy coverage for the public-posting assessment. Active protective measures with inadequate effect do not prove nonactivation. The Canadian regulator’s PIPEDA finding is preserved with its jurisdiction and broader scope, but no admitted canonical PIPEDA requirement exists and it is not relabelled as NIST, IEEE or EU compliance. The existing gap is retained without creating a new class. The privacy and preventive-filtering outcomes are Not aligned for the reported pathway. Safeguard evaluation, wider intervention and response processes remain Boundary where their decisive records are not available. The Canadian legal finding retains its own jurisdiction and scope. Later implementation claims and monitoring commitments do not demonstrate successful resolution. Reported findings about broad platform practices remain separate from the affected individual’s precise image and recovery.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The case tests three boundaries independently: control over identifiable likeness, the adequacy of an active protective posture against prohibited outputs, and risk assessment when a private image-generation capability is coupled to automatic public posting. The later regulator record makes those mechanisms assessable without assuming that a policy alone proved a functioning filter or that one remedial change settled the problem.
